title: One tail is enough to work on.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: The theorem permits every real A, and both matrix norms are unchanged by a sign.
state.goal: Control deviations both above and below the mean.

chosen.observation: Replacing A by −A turns Q into −Q without changing V or L. The lower tail is another instance of the same upper-tail problem.
chosen.move: Work backward from the two-sided endpoint. It suffices to obtain an upper-tail estimate for an arbitrary matrix, then apply it again to −A.
chosen.justification: The sign-reversal choice is strategic. Verifying the identity and the event union is basic. Numerical prefactors are adjusted at the end.
chosen.toolkit: Union bound; homogeneity of operator and Frobenius norms.

written: It suffices to bound ℙ(Q ≥ t). Indeed, replacing A by −A replaces Q by −Q and preserves both matrix norms. The same upper-tail estimate therefore applies to the lower tail, and the two estimates can be combined by the union bound.

title: Read the quadratic form coordinate by coordinate.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.goal: Find usable structure in the centered quadratic form.

chosen.observation: For i ≠ j, the given independence directly permits 𝔼(XᵢXⱼ) = 𝔼Xᵢ 𝔼Xⱼ = 0. This observation supports a basic inference, not a new strategic construction.
chosen.move: Expand what is already given. Independence and zero means eliminate off-diagonal terms from the expectation.
chosen.mathematics:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ
chosen.justification: The equality is direct expansion. Choosing to give D and S different proof methods is the next strategic decision.
chosen.toolkit: Expectation factorization for independent variables; linearity of expectation.

written: By independence and the mean-zero assumption, 𝔼(XᵢXⱼ) = 0 for i ≠ j. Consequently, Q = ∑ᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²) + ∑ᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ =: D + S.

title: Give the two kinds of terms different jobs.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: The identity Q = D + S. Terms in D use separate coordinates; terms in S can share them.
state.goal: A bound for ℙ(D + S ≥ t).

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

chosen.observation: Only the diagonal sum preserves independence term by term. Separating it lets Bernstein handle the easy branch while we develop a different tool for the cross terms.
chosen.move: The upper-tail goal branches. Bound D and S at threshold t/2. The diagonal branch is a side checkpoint; the main track follows the harder cross terms.
chosen.justification: This is a sufficient-condition reduction. D and S need not be independent. Choosing the split and thresholds is strategic; the event inclusion is basic logic.
chosen.toolkit: Union bound; knowledge of the input conditions for Bernstein and decoupling.

written: We estimate the two sums separately. Since D + S ≥ t implies that D ≥ t/2 or S ≥ t/2, ℙ(Q ≥ t) ≤ ℙ(D ≥ t/2) + ℙ(S ≥ t/2). No independence between D and S is required for this reduction.

title: Close the diagonal branch with Bernstein.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: Independent variables Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ², each with subexponential norm at most CK².
state.goal: An exponential bound for the diagonal sum D.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

chosen.observation: Bernstein accepts independent centered subexponential summands and produces exactly a minimum of quadratic and linear scales—the shape the endpoint asks for.
chosen.move: The square of a subgaussian is subexponential. Centering preserves that control, and the diagonal summands are independent.
chosen.mathematics:
‖Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²‖ψ₁ ≤ CK²
Σᵢ aᵢᵢ² ≤ ‖A‖F²,   maxᵢ ∣aᵢᵢ∣ ≤ ‖A‖
ℙ(D ≥ t/2) ≤ exp[−c min{t²/V, t/L}]
chosen.justification: Check independence, centering and subexponential sizes before applying Bernstein. If the diagonal is zero, D is zero and the positive-threshold bound is immediate.
chosen.toolkit: Subgaussian-square and subexponential-centering bounds; Bernstein inequality.

written: The variables Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ² are independent, centered, and subexponential, with ‖Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²‖ ψ₁ ≤ CK². Bernstein’s inequality, together with ∑ᵢ aᵢᵢ² ≤ ‖A‖ F ² and maxᵢ |aᵢᵢ| ≤ ‖A‖, yields ℙ(D ≥ t/2) ≤ exp[−c min{t²/V, t/L}]. If the diagonal of A is zero, this estimate holds directly because D = 0.

title: Ask for an exponential moment instead of a tail.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: The coordinates come with subgaussian exponential-moment bounds, but S itself has dependent summands.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

chosen.observation: Exponentiation turns a tail event into an expectation problem. A quadratic MGF bound gives the t²/V regime; a cutoff λ ≲ 1/L supplies the t/L regime.
chosen.move: Choose a transform whose expectation the toolkit can control. An MGF bound over a restricted parameter range will be enough.
chosen.mathematics:
ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.
chosen.justification: Apply Markov to the nonnegative variable exp(λS). This yields an upper bound, not equality between the tail and MGF. We will choose λ only after establishing its allowed range.

written: For the off-diagonal sum, fix λ > 0. Applying Markov’s inequality to exp(λS), we obtain ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼 exp(λS). We will prove that 𝔼 exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²) for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L, and then choose λ in that range.

title: Prepare the linear-form bound.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.goal: A reusable bound when the coefficients of a linear form become fixed.

chosen.observation: For a fixed vector v, exponentiating a sum makes a product. Independence factors its expectation, and the scalar subgaussian MGF applies to every factor.
chosen.move: The starting assumptions already control any fixed linear combination of the coordinates.
chosen.justification: The scalar MGF bound is an available theorem. Factoring the expectation, substituting its inputs, and summing the exponent are its verification steps. The mean-zero condition matters here.

written: For every fixed vector v and every real η, independence and the mean-zero subgaussian MGF estimate imply 𝔼 exp(η⟨X,v⟩) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼 exp(ηvᵢXᵢ) ≤ ∏ᵢ exp(CK²η²vᵢ²) = exp(CK²η²‖v‖₂²).

title: Make one side possible to hold fixed.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: S = Σᵢ≠ⱼaᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ. Shared coordinates block a direct independent-sum argument.
state.goal: Use linear-form MGF control on the cross terms.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.

chosen.observation: In XᵀAX, holding one copy of X fixed also freezes the other. In XᵀAX′, conditioning on X′ leaves a genuine random linear form in X.
chosen.move: Introduce an independent copy X′. Decoupling bounds the off-diagonal exponential moment by a bilinear form involving two independent vectors.
chosen.mathematics:
𝔼exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
Conditional on X′: XᵀAX′ = 〈X, AX′〉.
chosen.justification: This is a convex-function comparison, not equality in law. One construction randomly splits indices into disjoint groups: each off-diagonal pair survives with probability 1/4. Jensen and zero conditional means give the factor 4. The full A is allowed on the right by the off-diagonal version of the theorem.
chosen.toolkit: Decoupling, Theorem 6.1.1 and Remark 6.1.2; Jensen inequality.

written: Let X′ be an independent copy of X. The off-diagonal decoupling inequality, applied to the convex function s ↦ exp(λs), gives 𝔼 exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼 exp(4λXᵀAX′). The version used here permits the full matrix A on the right. Conditional on X′, the bilinear form XᵀAX′ is the linear form ⟨X,AX′⟩ with fixed coefficients.

title: Recognize a Gaussian formula inside the bound.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: After conditioning, v = AX′ is fixed, and a bound of the form exp(CK²λ²‖v‖²) is available.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.

𝔼exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
Conditional on X′: XᵀAX′ = 〈X, AX′〉.

chosen.observation: A Gaussian linear form has MGF exp(μ²‖v‖²/2). Choosing μ proportional to Kλ matches the entire expression, not just its general shape.
chosen.move: The decoupled expression suggests conditioning. Its conditional subgaussian upper bound has the same form as an exact Gaussian MGF.
chosen.mathematics:
𝔼g exp(μ〈g,v〉) = exp(μ²‖v‖²/2)
Choose μ = √(2C)Kλ.
New subgoal: bound 𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′), with θ = CK²λ.
chosen.justification: This step proposes the replacement and a new sufficient goal. The forward replacement must still verify the comparison in both arguments.
chosen.toolkit: Gaussian linear MGF; Gaussian replacement, Lemma 6.2.3.

written: Let g,g′ be independent standard Gaussian vectors, independent of X,X′. The Gaussian MGF identity is 𝔼 g exp(μ⟨g,v⟩) = exp(μ²‖v‖₂²/2). Choosing μ = √(2C)Kη matches the preceding subgaussian upper bound. Condition first on X′ and use v = AX′ to replace X by g. Average over X′, then condition on g and apply the same argument to X′. Absorbing the decoupling factor 4 into an absolute constant, we obtain 𝔼 exp(4λXᵀAX′) ≤ 𝔼 exp(C₁K²λgᵀAg′).

title: Carry out the two Gaussian replacements.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: The decoupled bilinear form and the fixed-coefficient subgaussian MGF bound.
state.goal: Transfer the MGF problem to a distribution whose rotations we understand.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.

𝔼exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
Conditional on X′: XᵀAX′ = 〈X, AX′〉.

𝔼exp(λ〈X,v〉) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼exp(λvᵢXᵢ)
≤ ∏ᵢ exp(CK²λ²vᵢ²)
= exp(CK²λ²‖v‖₂²)

chosen.observation: Each replacement becomes a one-vector linear-form calculation when the other vector is fixed. Two such comparisons produce a parameter of order K²λ.
chosen.move: Condition on X′ and use the prepared linear bound to replace X by g at cost CK. Then condition on g and replace X′ by an independent g′ at another cost CK.
chosen.mathematics:
𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
≤ 𝔼exp(CK²λ gᵀAg′),
g,g′ independent standard Gaussian vectors.
chosen.justification: Iterated expectation lifts each conditional comparison. Constants absorb the factor 4 from decoupling. No coordinate-wise equality in distribution between X and g is claimed.
chosen.toolkit: Subgaussian linear MGF; Gaussian MGF; iterated expectation.

written: Let g,g′ be independent standard Gaussian vectors, independent of X,X′. The Gaussian MGF identity is 𝔼 g exp(μ⟨g,v⟩) = exp(μ²‖v‖₂²/2). Choosing μ = √(2C)Kη matches the preceding subgaussian upper bound. Condition first on X′ and use v = AX′ to replace X by g. Average over X′, then condition on g and apply the same argument to X′. Absorbing the decoupling factor 4 into an absolute constant, we obtain 𝔼 exp(4λXᵀAX′) ≤ 𝔼 exp(C₁K²λgᵀAg′).

title: Rotate until the matrix exposes independent products.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: Independent standard Gaussian vectors and a fixed matrix A.
state.goal: A Gaussian MGF controlled by ‖A‖F and ‖A‖.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.

𝔼exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
Conditional on X′: XᵀAX′ = 〈X, AX′〉.

𝔼g exp(μ〈g,v〉) = exp(μ²‖v‖²/2)
Choose μ = √(2C)Kλ.
New subgoal: bound 𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′), with θ = CK²λ.

𝔼exp(λ〈X,v〉) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼exp(λvᵢXᵢ)
≤ ∏ᵢ exp(CK²λ²vᵢ²)
= exp(CK²λ²‖v‖₂²)

𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
≤ 𝔼exp(CK²λ gᵀAg′),
g,g′ independent standard Gaussian vectors.

chosen.observation: An arbitrary rotation could destroy independence for the original X. Gaussian rotation preserves independent standard coordinates. The resulting singular values give both target norms.
chosen.move: Choose the singular value decomposition A = U diag(sᵢ)Vᵀ. The Gaussian subgoal becomes a product of scalar MGFs.
chosen.mathematics:
gᵀAg′ ≡in law Σᵢ sᵢgᵢgᵢ′
𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼exp(θsᵢgᵢgᵢ′)
Σᵢsᵢ² = ‖A‖F²,   maxᵢsᵢ = ‖A‖.
chosen.justification: SVD is valid for a nonsymmetric real A too: use Uᵀg and Vᵀg′. Their independent standard Gaussian laws are preserved. This is why replacement precedes rotation.
chosen.toolkit: SVD; Gaussian rotation invariance; independence; singular-value norm identities.

written: Write A = U diag(sᵢ)Rᵀ. By Gaussian rotation invariance, Uᵀg and Rᵀg′ remain independent standard Gaussian vectors. Therefore gᵀAg′ has the same distribution as ∑ᵢ sᵢgᵢgᵢ′, and independence of the pairs gives 𝔼 exp(θgᵀAg′) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼 exp(θsᵢgᵢgᵢ′).

title: Compute the scalar MGF and its domain.

state.assumptions: Independent coordinates, zero means, and scalar subgaussian control K. Also the fixed matrix A, its operator norm, and its Frobenius norm.
state.scope: For the displayed derivation assume t > 0 and V,L > 0. The zero cases are immediate. Definitions and calculation are basic; choosing a useful representation or theorem is strategic.
state.facts: Independent pairs (gᵢ,gᵢ′) and the representation Σᵢsᵢgᵢgᵢ′.
state.goal: The product bound anticipated by the goal layer.

prerequisites.statement:
Q = D + S
D = Σᵢ aᵢᵢ(Xᵢ² − 𝔼Xᵢ²)
S = Σᵢ≠ⱼ aᵢⱼXᵢXⱼ

ℙ(S ≥ t/2) ≤ exp(−λt/2) 𝔼exp(λS)
New goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²)
for 0 < λ ≤ c₀/L.

𝔼exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
Conditional on X′: XᵀAX′ = 〈X, AX′〉.

𝔼g exp(μ〈g,v〉) = exp(μ²‖v‖²/2)
Choose μ = √(2C)Kλ.
New subgoal: bound 𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′), with θ = CK²λ.

𝔼exp(λ〈X,v〉) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼exp(λvᵢXᵢ)
≤ ∏ᵢ exp(CK²λ²vᵢ²)
= exp(CK²λ²‖v‖₂²)

𝔼exp(4λXᵀAX′)
≤ 𝔼exp(CK²λ gᵀAg′),
g,g′ independent standard Gaussian vectors.

gᵀAg′ ≡in law Σᵢ sᵢgᵢgᵢ′
𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′) = ∏ᵢ 𝔼exp(θsᵢgᵢgᵢ′)
Σᵢsᵢ² = ‖A‖F²,   maxᵢsᵢ = ‖A‖.

chosen.observation: The exponent is linear in gᵢ′ when gᵢ is fixed. Its conditional MGF becomes exp(u²gᵢ²/2), whose expectation is explicit.
chosen.move: The scalar target now has a direct calculation. Conditioning once reduces it to the MGF of a squared Gaussian.
chosen.mathematics:
𝔼exp(ugg′) = (1 − u²)⁻¹ᐟ²
≤ exp(u²)  when u² ≤ 1/2.
𝔼exp(θgᵀAg′) ≤ exp(θ²‖A‖F²)
for ∣θ∣ ≤ 1/(√2 ‖A‖).
chosen.justification: The bound uses −½log(1−u²) ≤ u² on [0,1/2]. The largest singular value controls the admissible θ; the sum of squares controls the exponent. Both are necessary.
chosen.toolkit: Gaussian linear and square MGFs; the elementary logarithm bound.

written: For independent scalar standard Gaussians g₁,g₁′, conditioning on g₁ and then using the MGF of g₁² gives 𝔼 exp(ug₁g₁′) = 𝔼 exp(u²g₁²/2) = (1 − u²) −1/2 ≤ exp(u²),   u² ≤ 1/2. Here the inequality follows from −½ log(1−z) ≤ z for 0 ≤ z ≤ 1/2. Substituting u = θsᵢ in each factor, and using ∑ᵢsᵢ² = ‖A‖ F ² and maxᵢsᵢ = ‖A‖, yields 𝔼 exp(θgᵀAg′) ≤ exp(θ²‖A‖ F ²), |θ| ≤ 1/(√2 ‖A‖).

state.facts: Decoupling, Gaussian replacement, and the computed Gaussian-product MGF.
state.goal: 𝔼exp(λS) ≤ exp(CVλ²) for λ at most c₀/L.

≤ ∏ᵢ exp(CK²λ²vᵢ²)

≤ exp(u²)  when u² ≤ 1/2.

chosen.observation: The forward chain has produced exactly the kind of bound requested by the backward Chernoff goal—including the parameter restriction. This checkpoint can now be discharged.
chosen.move: Substitute θ = CK²λ into the Gaussian estimate, and chain it with the two forward comparisons. This is the main connection between the two layers.
chosen.mathematics:
𝔼 exp(λS) ≤ 𝔼 exp(4λXᵀAX′)
≤ 𝔼 exp(CK²λgᵀAg′)
≤ exp(CK⁴λ²‖A‖F²) = exp(CVλ²),
for ∣λ∣ ≤ c₀/(K²‖A‖) = c₀/L.
chosen.justification: The constant c₀ includes all rescalings. A domain restriction on θ must be converted into a domain restriction on λ; it cannot be dropped.
chosen.toolkit: The three established estimates; substitution and inequality transitivity.

written: Combining decoupling, replacement, and the Gaussian estimate with θ = C₁K²λ proves 𝔼 exp(λS) ≤ exp(CK⁴λ²‖A‖ F ²) = exp(CVλ²),   |λ| ≤ c₀/L. The absolute constant c₀ accounts for the parameter rescaling. This is the exponential-moment estimate required above.

title: Balance the exponent, respecting the cutoff.

state.goal: Turn the exponential-moment estimate into the desired tail.

chosen.observation: The only remaining mismatch is the prefactor: splitting terms and signs gives 4 instead of 2. Combining with the universal bound ℙ ≤ 1 absorbs it into a smaller exponent constant.
chosen.move: Combine the diagonal and off-diagonal tails. Apply the same result to −A and use the union bound. Every goal checkpoint is now supported.
chosen.justification: For q ≤ 2log(2)/c the last expression is at least 1; for larger q the comparison with 4exp(−cq) holds. The theorem follows for all t; degenerate cases were handled at the start.

written: Combining the bounds for D and S gives the upper-tail estimate for Q. Apply the same argument to −A and add the two tail probabilities. With q = min{t²/V,t/L}, this gives ℙ(|Q| ≥ t) ≤ min{1, 4 exp(−cq)} ≤ 2 exp(−cq/2). Indeed, when q ≤ 2 log(2)/c the last expression is at least 1; otherwise it bounds 4 exp(−cq). Renaming c/2 as c establishes the stated inequality. □
